Drew
drū
v. (preterite of draw: pulled, drew out, approached; rendering Hebrew mashah and nagash, Greek helko and eggizo)
Preterite of draw, from the Saxon dragan, to pull or drag. Hebrew mashah is to draw out of water, and Pharaoh's daughter names Moses from it; nagash is to draw near, especially to approach God, and it is the priestly word for approach.

Biblical Definition

Drew covers pulling, drawing out, and drawing near, and Scripture uses all three theologically. The drawing out of water names the deliverer: Pharaoh's daughter “called his name Moses: and she said, Because I drew him out of the water” (Exodus 2:10) — a name that will describe his life's work, since the man drawn out of the Nile draws a nation out of the sea. The drawing of a sword marks the failure of the flesh to defend the kingdom: in Gethsemane one of them “stretched out his hand, and drew his sword, and struck a servant of the high priest” (Matthew 26:51), and our Lord healed the wound and told him to put it up, for they that take the sword shall perish with the sword. The most tender use is the drawing near of the risen Christ to men who did not know him: while the two on the Emmaus road “communed together and reasoned, Jesus himself drew near, and went with them” (Luke 24:15). He does not begin with the disclosure but with the company, and expounds the Scriptures before he breaks the bread. The verb also carries the doctrine of effectual calling, for no man can come to Christ except the Father draw him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Preterite of draw — pulled, drew out, drew near. Moses was drawn out of the water, Peter drew a sword and was rebuked, and the risen Christ drew near to men who did not know him.

DREW, pret. of draw. [Sax. dragan, to pull.] Pulled; hauled; dragged along.

2. Pulled out; extracted; as, he drew his sword; she drew water from the well.

3. Attracted; allured; as, the multitude was drawn after him.

4. Approached; came near; as, the time drew nigh.

5. In Scripture, of effectual calling; no man can come to me, except the Father draw him, John 6.

Key Scripture

Exodus 2:10 — "And the child grew, and she brought him unto Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. And she called his name Moses: and she said, Because I drew him out of the water. Moses: that is, Drawn out"

Matthew 26:51 — "And, behold, one of them which were with Jesus stretched out his hand, and drew his sword, and struck a servant of the high priest's, and smote off his ear."

Luke 24:15 — "And it came to pass, that, while they communed together and reasoned, Jesus himself drew near, and went with them."

Psalm 34:4 — "I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The pressure is doctrinal rather than lexical: the drawing of John 6:44 is commonly softened into a general influence that men may finally refuse.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word's ordinary senses are stable. What is contested is one text, and the contest matters. In John 6:44 our Lord says no man can come to him except the Father draw him, and the verb helko is the word used of drawing a net full of fishes to shore and of Paul and Silas being dragged into the marketplace. It is not persuasion offered and possibly declined; and the same verse ends by promising that everyone so drawn will be raised up at the last day, which makes the drawing effectual by definition, since the group drawn and the group raised are one group.

The principle to recover is that this doctrine is a comfort rather than a threat, and Luke 24:15 shows why. The two on the Emmaus road were not seeking a risen Christ; they were leaving Jerusalem disappointed, saying they had trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel. He drew near to them. Effectual calling looks like that from the inside — not coercion, but a companion on the road who opens the Scriptures until the heart burns.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mashah is to draw out of water, the root of the name Moses; nagash is to draw near, the priestly approach word. Greek helko is to drag or draw with force, and eggizo is to come near.

expand to see more

Hebrew mashah (H4871) — to draw out of water; the root of the name Moses in Exodus 2:10.

Hebrew nagash (H5066) — to draw near, to approach; used of priestly approach to the altar.

Hebrew mashak (H4900) — to draw, to drag; with lovingkindness have I drawn thee, Jeremiah 31:3.

Greek helko (G1670) — to draw, to drag; the verb of John 6:44 and of hauling in a full net.

Greek eggizo (G1448) — to draw near; draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you.

Usage

"Of the deliverer drawn from the water: because I drew him out of the water (Exodus 2:10)."

"Of the flesh defending the kingdom by force: drew his sword, and struck a servant of the high priest (Matthew 26:51)."

"Of the risen Christ approaching the discouraged: Jesus himself drew near, and went with them (Luke 24:15)."
